stem: How did the railroads help destroy the buffalo herds in the 1870s and 1880s?

stimulus.source_note: Colonel Richard Dodge's 1871 description as quoted in HISTORY.com, "Why Is the Bison America's National Mammal?"; herd figures from the U.S. Geological Survey (about 20-30 million bison before the slaughter, barely more than 1,000 by 1889) and Hornaday's 1889 census count of 1,091.
stimulus.text:
"The whole country appeared one mass of buffalo," wrote Colonel Richard Dodge when he traveled the Santa Fe Trail in 1871.

(Background from the books: between 1871 and 1883, hide hunters working in teams killed millions of bison for their skins, and railroads carried the hides east. When the Smithsonian sent an expedition to Montana in 1886 to collect specimens from the vanishing herds, few remained; Hornaday's 1889 census counted only 1,091 bison left in all of North America.)

options.text: Railroad companies bought the herds and moved them to eastern zoos
options.misconception: Background: no railroad bought herds for zoos; the herds were slaughtered for hides, not collected.

options.text: Railroads moved hunters and hides, and crews shot buffalo from the trains
Railroads fenced the entire Plains so the buffalo starved inside the fences
options.misconception: Background: fences came later, for cattle and farms; the buffalo were killed by hunters, not starved behind fences.

options.text: Railroads poisoned the rivers the buffalo drank from
options.misconception: Background: no poisoning campaign existed; the killing was done with rifles, by hunters and train crews.

rationales.A: Background: the herds were not collected, they were killed. Hides by the million went east on the rails; live buffalo did not.
rationales.B: Background from the books: railroad workers and passengers shot buffalo for food and sport, hide hunters rode the rails to the herds, and the railroads carried the hides to eastern markets.
rationales.C: Background: barbed wire fenced cattle range and farms in the 1870s and 1880s, but the buffalo fell to rifles years before fences covered the Plains.
rationales.D: Background: the slaughter was shooting, not poisoning. Teams of sharpshooters and skinners did the work, and the trains moved the product.
rationales.general:
The railroad did not just cross the buffalo country; it brought the hunters and took the hides.
1. Start with the train itself: crews and passengers shot buffalo from the cars for food and sport.
2. Add the freight. Background: hide hunters used the rails to reach the herds, and the rails carried millions of hides east.
3. Count the result. Background: the herds fell from about 30 million animals to barely more than 1,000 by 1889.
Remember: a railroad moves whatever pays, and in the 1870s hides paid.
